Lessons.Title: Sequences are Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Define sequences as integer-domain functions, specify initial conditions and write recursive function notation.

For a triangular dot pattern with one dot at step 1 and a new row of n dots at step n, the count is D(1)=1 and D(n)=D(n-1)+n for whole-number n>=2. The first five counts are 1,3,6,10,15 and the explicit formula is n(n+1)/2. Its differences increase, so it is neither arithmetic nor geometric. A recursive equation without a starting term is incomplete.

First-party independent cool-down: A triangular display starts with one dot. On each next step add a new row containing as many dots as the step number. Write D(1), D(n) for n>=2, list D(1)...D(5), and explain whether it is arithmetic or geometric. Answer key: D(1)=1, D(n)=D(n-1)+n; 1,3,6,10,15; neither.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sequence as function
KeyConcepts.Definition: An integer-indexed function has one output for each permitted input n.
KeyConcepts.Example: D: positive integers to nonnegative integers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Recursive notation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A term is defined through an earlier term.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For n>=2, f(n)=f(n-1)+d, with f(1) specified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonlinear triangular numbers
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each new triangle row adds its row number.

WorkedExamples.Title: Triangular pattern
WorkedExamples.Question: How many dots are there at step 5?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the previous count and add the new row.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare recursive sequences
WorkedExamples.Question: Classify 30,40,50,... and 1,3,7,15,...
Steps: The first has constant +10, hence arithmetic.
The second has differences 2,4,8 so not arithmetic.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The first is arithmetic; second is neither.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a sequence rule as context-free.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It can alter the index, initial term, units or learning target.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the beginning term, domain and original lesson model.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a fixed common difference when the sequence is not arithmetic.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Differing consecutive differences invalidate the arithmetic formula.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Calculate two or more differences or ratios before selecting a rule.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Auto-grading graphs, card exchanges or manipulative proof from a number alone.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Numeric equality does not establish a correct diagram or explanation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a teacher rubric for visual and reasoning evidence.
